claims.text: Nearly equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are the material under study.
The FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have controlled diameters of approximately 3–6.5 nm.
The nanoparticles are uniformly distributed on an inert SiN membrane.
Combining in situ heating aberration-corrected STEM with molecular dynamics simulations can be used to investigate the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Nanoparticle thermal behavior can be investigated over a temperature range extending from ambient temperature to 973 K.
The in situ heating measurements are performed under high-vacuum conditions.
Particles of different sizes are experimentally compared to determine size-dependent thermal behavior.
Nanoparticle size controls the surface-to-volume ratio.
The size-dependent surface-to-volume ratio affects atomic diffusion rates and the onset of phase segregation or melting.
Elevated temperature promotes atomic diffusion and can drive progressive phase separation in quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo faster surface diffusion than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles nucleate phase segregation, surface melting, or other structural rearrangements earlier than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower thermal stability than larger nanoparticles.
In situ STEM will show structural or chemical changes in smaller FeCuCrCoNi particles at lower temperatures than in larger particles.
Molecular dynamics simulations will show enhanced diffusion and earlier instability in smaller FeCuCrCoNi particles.
The as-deposited FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are initially uniform and single-phase.
Substrate interactions or surface contamination can modify the observed thermal behavior.
The instability-onset temperature can vary with composition, particle shape, and experimental conditions.
